title: 06 — App Service & Hosting Choices
html:
06 — App Service & Hosting Choices

Where your .NET code actually runs. App Service is still the default for a .NET web API; this file covers it properly, then the alternatives and how to choose.

1. Choosing a compute service

flowchart TD
    A[New .NET workload] --> B{Event-driven, spiky,<br/>short-lived executions?}
    B -->|Yes| F["Azure Functions<br/>(Flex Consumption)"]
    B -->|No| C{Standard HTTP API or web app,<br/>no exotic infrastructure needs?}
    C -->|Yes| D{Need containers, KEDA scaling,<br/>Dapr, or scale-to-zero?}
    D -->|No| AS["⭐ App Service<br/>the default for .NET web apps"]
    D -->|Yes| CA["Container Apps"]
    C -->|No| E{Many services, custom networking,<br/>service mesh, AND a platform team?}
    E -->|Yes| AKS["AKS"]
    E -->|No| AS
Service Best for Avoid when
App Service Web apps and APIs. Slots, easy scaling, managed certificates, minimal ops You need pod-level control or a service mesh
Container Apps Containerised microservices, KEDA event-driven scaling, scale to zero, Dapr You need raw Kubernetes APIs
Azure Functions Event-driven and scheduled work, glue, bursty workloads Long-running steady workloads (cost), strict cold-start SLAs
AKS Many services, complex networking, multi-tenant scheduling, portability You don't have a platform team — the operational surface is a full-time job
Container Instances One-off container runs, CI agents, simple sidecars Anything needing scaling or ingress
Virtual Machines Lift-and-shift, legacy dependencies, licensed software Anything greenfield

💡 The honest default for a .NET team without a platform team is App Service (or Container Apps if you've containerised). Count the things AKS gives you that you'd otherwise have to build; if it's fewer than the operational tasks it adds, don't.

2. App Service plans

The plan is the compute you pay for; apps run on it. Multiple apps can share a plan — they then share CPU and memory, which is convenient in dev and a noisy-neighbour problem in production.

Tier Use Notes
F1 Free / D1 Shared Experiments Quotas, no custom domain SSL, no Always On
B1–B3 Basic Dev/test Manual scale only, no slots on B1 🔄, no autoscale
S1–S3 Standard Light production 5 slots, autoscale, daily backups
P0v3–P5v3 Premium v3 ⭐ Production More memory per core, faster storage, zone redundancy, 20 slots, VNet integration
Isolated v2 (ASE v3) Regulatory isolation, private-only Expensive; a dedicated deployment stamp

Sizing guidance: start at P1v3 for a production API and scale from measured data. ⚠️ The most common waste in Azure is a P2v3/P3v3 plan running at 8% CPU because someone sized for fear. The most common outage is a B1 in production with no Always On and no slots.

resource plan 'Microsoft.Web/serverfarms@2023-12-01' = {
  name: 'asp-shop-prod'
  sku: { name: 'P1v3', capacity: 2 }     // ≥2 instances: survives an instance restart
  properties: {
    reserved: true                        // Linux
    zoneRedundant: true                   // ⭐ survives a datacentre failure
  }
}

💡 Always run ≥2 instances in production. One instance means every platform restart, scale operation, or host update is an outage.

3. ⭐ Deployment slots — the zero-downtime mechanism

A slot is a fully functional app with its own hostname running on the same plan. Deploy to staging, warm it up, verify, then swap — which changes the load-balancer routing, so it's near-instantaneous.

Before swap:                          After swap:
production  ← v1 (live traffic)       production  ← v2 (live traffic)
staging     ← v2 (warmed)             staging     ← v1  ← ⭐ your instant rollback

3.1 What a swap actually does

sequenceDiagram
    participant P as Production slot
    participant S as Staging slot
    Note over S: 1. Apply production's slot-STICKY settings to staging
    Note over S: 2. Restart staging with those settings
    Note over S: 3. WARM UP — Azure sends HTTP requests to the warm-up path
    Note over S: 4. Wait for healthy responses
    P->>S: 5. Swap the routing rules (near-instant)
    Note over P,S: staging now holds the OLD version — swap again to roll back

The critical detail most people miss: step 1 restarts the staging slot with production's configuration. So the instance that goes live has already started up with production settings and connection strings — that's what makes the swap safe, and it's also why the swap takes a minute rather than being truly instant.

3.2 Sticky vs swapped settings

Stays with the slot (sticky) Swaps with the code
App settings marked "deployment slot setting" App settings not marked sticky
Connection strings marked sticky Connection strings not marked sticky
Publishing endpoints, custom domains, TLS bindings General settings (framework version, always-on, 32/64-bit)
Scale settings, WAF, private endpoints Handler mappings, monitoring settings
Managed identity ⚠️ (each slot has its own) App Service Authentication

⚠️ The classic slot bug: the staging slot's connection string points at the staging database. It isn't marked as a slot setting, so after the swap production is running against the staging database. Mark every environment-specific setting as a slot setting, and prefer Key Vault references keyed by slot.

3.3 Warm-up — the difference between a good swap and a bad one

Without warm-up, the swap succeeds but the first users hit a cold .NET app: JIT compilation, DI container construction, EF model building, cache population. You get a burst of slow requests or timeouts right after every deploy.

App setting:  WEBSITE_SWAP_WARMUP_PING_PATH      = /health/ready
App setting:  WEBSITE_SWAP_WARMUP_PING_STATUSES  = 200,202
App setting:  WEBSITE_WARMUP_PATH                = /health/ready   (for scale-out too)

The default warm-up path is /. Point it at a health endpoint that actually exercises your dependencies and primes your caches — not a static file that returns 200 regardless.

// A warm-up endpoint that does real work
app.MapGet("/health/ready", async (AppDbContext db, IMemoryCache cache, CancellationToken ct) =>
{
    await db.Database.CanConnectAsync(ct);            // opens a pooled connection, builds the EF model
    await WarmCachesAsync(cache, ct);                 // prime reference data
    return Results.Ok(new { status = "ready" });
});

On Windows App Service you can additionally use IIS application initialization in web.config:

<system.webServer>
  <applicationInitialization doAppStart="true">
    <add initializationPage="/health/ready" />
    <add initializationPage="/api/warmup" />
  </applicationInitialization>
</system.webServer>

💡 Also enable "Always On" on both slots. Without it, an idle app is unloaded after ~20 minutes and the next request pays a full cold start — and swap readiness becomes unpredictable.

💡 "Swap with preview" applies production settings to staging and pauses, letting you verify the app under production configuration before completing the swap. Use it for high-risk releases.

3.4 Traffic routing (poor man's canary)

az webapp traffic-routing set -g rg-shop-prod -n app-shop-api \
  --distribution staging=10        # 10% of traffic to the new version

Users are pinned with a cookie (x-ms-routing-name) so they stay on one version. Watch the metrics, then ramp or revert. ⚠️ This is coarse — no automatic metric gating. For real canary analysis use Azure Front Door, Container Apps revisions, or a deployment controller.

4. Configuration

Precedence in ASP.NET Core (later wins): appsettings.json → appsettings.{Environment}.json → user secrets (dev) → environment variables → command line → Key Vault provider.

App Service App settings become environment variables, which is how they override your JSON files.

Portal setting name          →  Configuration key
ConnectionStrings__Default   →  ConnectionStrings:Default
Pricing__TimeoutSeconds      →  Pricing:TimeoutSeconds

⚠️ Use double underscore __ for nesting. On Linux, colons are not valid in environment variable names — Pricing:TimeoutSeconds silently won't bind.

4.1 ⭐ Key Vault references — secrets without any code

App setting value:
@Microsoft.KeyVault(SecretUri=https://kv-shop-prod.vault.azure.net/secrets/SqlPassword/)

App Service resolves this at startup using the app's managed identity and injects the plain value as an environment variable. Your code just reads configuration — it never knows Key Vault exists.

Requirements: the app has a managed identity, and that identity has Key Vault Secrets User on the vault (or the slot's identity, separately). ⚠️ Resolution happens at startup and on configuration change — rotating the secret in Key Vault does not automatically update a running app unless you reference it without a version and the platform refreshes it 🔄. For genuinely dynamic refresh, use Azure App Configuration with a sentinel key (file 10).

🧪 A failed reference shows in the portal's app-settings blade with a red status and the app usually fails to start — check the status column first when an app won't boot after a config change.

4.2 Settings you should set on every production app

Setting Value Why
ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT Production Detailed errors off, correct config file
WEBSITE_RUN_FROM_PACKAGE 1 ⭐ Atomic deploys, read-only file system, faster cold start
WEBSITE_SWAP_WARMUP_PING_PATH /health/ready §3.3
APPLICATIONINSIGHTS_CONNECTION_STRING from the AI resource Telemetry
WEBSITE_TIME_ZONE e.g. GMT Standard Time ⚠️ Default is UTC; only set this if you truly need local time (usually you don't — keep UTC and convert at the edge)
DOTNET_gcServer 1 Server GC for throughput (usually the default in the container)
WEBSITE_HEALTHCHECK_MAXPINGFAILURES 3 With Health Check configured, unhealthy instances are replaced

Health Check (Settings → Health check) removes an unhealthy instance from the load balancer and eventually replaces it. Point it at a /health/live-style endpoint. ⚠️ Don't point it at a check that fails when your database is down — you'd take every instance out of rotation during a transient database blip and turn a degradation into an outage.

5. Scaling

Scale up (vertical) Scale out (horizontal)
What Bigger plan tier More instances
Limit Tier ceiling Plan maximum (Premium v3: 30 by default 🔄)
Requires Nothing Statelessness 
// Autoscale on a real signal, with a scale-in cooldown to prevent flapping
resource autoscale 'Microsoft.Insights/autoscalesettings@2022-10-01' = {
  name: 'autoscale-shop-prod'
  properties: {
    targetResourceUri: plan.id
    profiles: [{
      name: 'default'
      capacity: { minimum: '2', maximum: '10', default: '2' }
      rules: [
        {
          metricTrigger: {
            metricName: 'CpuPercentage', metricResourceUri: plan.id
            timeGrain: 'PT1M', statistic: 'Average'
            timeWindow: 'PT5M', timeAggregation: 'Average'
            operator: 'GreaterThan', threshold: 70
          }
          scaleAction: { direction: 'Increase', type: 'ChangeCount', value: '2', cooldown: 'PT5M' }
        }
        {
          metricTrigger: {
            metricName: 'CpuPercentage', metricResourceUri: plan.id
            timeGrain: 'PT1M', statistic: 'Average'
            timeWindow: 'PT10M', timeAggregation: 'Average'   // longer window on scale-in
            operator: 'LessThan', threshold: 30
          }
          scaleAction: { direction: 'Decrease', type: 'ChangeCount', value: '1', cooldown: 'PT10M' }
        }
      ]
    }]
  }
}

Autoscale rules that work: scale out fast, in slow (asymmetric thresholds and cooldowns) to avoid flapping; scale on the metric that actually reflects load (CPU, HTTP queue length, or a custom metric like queue depth); and add scheduled profiles for predictable patterns (business hours, month-end).

⚠️ Autoscale is not instant — a new instance takes a minute or two to provision and warm up. For a known spike (a marketing launch, a market open), pre-scale on a schedule.

What breaks when you scale out — the checklist:

  • In-memory session or cache → move to Redis, or accept per-instance divergence with a short TTL
  • In-memory scheduled jobs (Timer, Quartz in-process) → they now run N times. Use a distributed scheduler or leader election
  • SignalR without a backplane → messages only reach clients on the same instance (file 08)
  • Local file writes → use Blob Storage
  • Singleton state, in-process locks → move to a distributed lock or a database constraint

⚠️ ARR Affinity (session affinity) is ON by default. It pins a user to an instance with a cookie, which defeats even load distribution and breaks gracefully-draining deploys. Turn it off unless you have in-memory session state — and if you do, fix that instead.

6. Networking for App Service

Feature Direction Purpose
VNet integration Outbound The app reaches private endpoints, on-prem, or private SQL
Private endpoint Inbound The app itself becomes reachable only from the VNet
Access restrictions Inbound IP allow-list / service tag rules
Hybrid connections Outbound Reach a specific on-prem host:port without a VPN
NAT Gateway Outbound ⭐ A static outbound IP for partner firewall allow-lists

⚠️ Two failures that consume an afternoon each:

  1. Private endpoint without private DNS. The app resolves the public name, gets a public IP, and the connection times out. You need the privatelink.* DNS zone linked to the VNet.
  2. App Service outbound IPs change when you scale or change tier. Never give a partner your app's outbound IP list — put a NAT Gateway in front.

Typical production topology:

Internet → Front Door (WAF, global LB, TLS) → App Service (access restricted to Front Door)
                                                   │ VNet integration
                                                   ▼
                                        Private endpoints: SQL, Key Vault, Storage, Service Bus

💡 Restrict the App Service to accept traffic only from your Front Door instance (using the AzureFrontDoor.Backend service tag plus the X-Azure-FDID header check) — otherwise attackers can bypass the WAF by hitting *.azurewebsites.net directly.

7. Deployment methods

Method Notes
Run From Package (WEBSITE_RUN_FROM_PACKAGE=1) ⭐ Default choice. Atomic, read-only wwwroot, faster cold start, no partial-file states
Zip Deploy Extracts files into wwwroot; simple, but non-atomic
Container Deploy an image from ACR; use a digest or an immutable tag, never latest
GitHub Actions / Azure Pipelines tasks What you'll actually use — they wrap the above
FTP/FTPS ⚠️ Disable it (ftpsState: 'Disabled')
Local Git / Kudu build Builds on the app instance — slow, and it puts a build toolchain in production. Avoid

💡 Always deploy to a slot and swap, never directly to production, even for "small" changes. The slot is also your rollback.

8. Container Apps (the modern middle ground)

Serverless Kubernetes without Kubernetes: you get revisions, KEDA-based scaling (including scale to zero), Dapr, ingress, and managed certificates — without operating a cluster.

resource app 'Microsoft.App/containerApps@2024-03-01' = {
  name: 'ca-shop-api'
  identity: { type: 'SystemAssigned' }
  properties: {
    managedEnvironmentId: env.id
    configuration: {
      ingress: { external: true, targetPort: 8080, transport: 'auto' }   // 'auto' enables HTTP/2 & gRPC
      registries: [{ server: 'crshop.azurecr.io', identity: 'system' }]  // ACR via managed identity
    }
    template: {
      containers: [{
        name: 'api'
        image: 'crshop.azurecr.io/shop-api@sha256:...'      // digest, not a tag
        resources: { cpu: json('0.5'), memory: '1Gi' }
        probes: [
          { type: 'Liveness',  httpGet: { path: '/health/live',  port: 8080 } }
          { type: 'Readiness', httpGet: { path: '/health/ready', port: 8080 } }
        ]
      }]
      scale: {
        minReplicas: 1                    // 0 for scale-to-zero; accept cold start
        maxReplicas: 10
        rules: [{
          name: 'queue-depth'
          custom: {                        // ⭐ KEDA: scale on Service Bus queue length
            type: 'azure-servicebus'
            metadata: { queueName: 'trades', messageCount: '20' }
            identity: 'system'
          }
        }]
      }
    }
  }
}

Key concepts: revisions (each config/image change creates one; you can split traffic between them for a real canary), environment (the shared boundary — VNet, Log Analytics, Dapr), and KEDA scalers (queue depth, HTTP concurrency, cron, and dozens more).

Container Apps vs App Service: choose Container Apps when you want scale-to-zero, event-driven (non-HTTP) scaling, per-revision traffic splitting, or Dapr. Choose App Service for a straightforward web app where slots and simplicity win.

9. Custom domains, TLS, and Front Door

az webapp config hostname add -g rg-shop-prod --webapp-name app-shop-api --hostname api.example.com
az webapp config ssl create   -g rg-shop-prod --name app-shop-api --hostname api.example.com  # App Service Managed Certificate — free, auto-renewing
az webapp update -g rg-shop-prod -n app-shop-api --https-only true
Option Notes
App Service Managed Certificate ⭐ Free, auto-renews. Doesn't support wildcards or apex domains in all cases 🔄
Key Vault certificate Bring your own; App Service auto-syncs renewals
Front Door / App Gateway managed cert TLS terminated at the edge

⚠️ Set the minimum TLS version to 1.2 (1.3 where supported) and disable FTPS. Both are simple settings that show up on every security review.

Azure Front Door adds global load balancing, WAF, caching, and edge TLS. Use it when you have users in multiple geographies, need a WAF, or want a stable anycast entry point. For a single-region internal app, it's usually unnecessary cost and complexity.

10. Diagnostics and troubleshooting

Tool Use
Diagnose and solve problems (portal) ⭐ Start here. Automated detectors for restarts, high CPU/memory, failed requests, slow responses
Log stream Live stdout/stderr — enable App Service logs first
Kudu / SCM console (https://<app>.scm.azurewebsites.net) File system, environment variables, process explorer, dump collection
Application Insights The real diagnostic surface (file 12)
Metrics CPU, memory, response time, HTTP 5xx, HTTP queue length, connections
Symptom Likely cause
App won't start after deploy A Key Vault reference failed to resolve; a missing app setting; a startup exception — check Log stream and the app settings blade status
502/503 after deploy Startup too slow, or no warm-up on the swap; check the health check path
Slow first request after idle Always On is off
High memory then recycle A leak, or a 32-bit worker process (switch to 64-bit)
Intermittent 500s only on some requests One unhealthy instance — enable Health Check so it's replaced
Works in staging, fails in production after swap A slot setting that should have been sticky (or vice versa)
Can't reach the database VNet integration missing, private DNS missing, or the SQL firewall doesn't allow Azure services
Outbound calls to a partner rejected Outbound IP changed — use a NAT Gateway

🧪

az webapp log tail -g rg-shop-prod -n app-shop-api
az webapp log deployment show -g rg-shop-prod -n app-shop-api
az webapp show -g rg-shop-prod -n app-shop-api --query "state"

11. Checklist

  • Premium v3 plan, zone redundant, ≥2 instances in production
  • httpsOnly: true, min TLS 1.2, FTPS disabled
  • Managed identity enabled — on the app and every slot
  • Staging slot; deploy → warm up → verify → swap → verify → swap back on failure
  • WEBSITE_SWAP_WARMUP_PING_PATH pointing at a real readiness endpoint
  • Always On enabled on production and staging slots
  • Environment-specific settings marked as slot settings
  • Secrets via Key Vault references, not literal values
  • WEBSITE_RUN_FROM_PACKAGE=1
  • Health Check configured, pointing at a liveness endpoint that doesn't hard-fail on shared dependencies
  • ARR affinity disabled (unless you genuinely need it — then fix the state instead)
  • Autoscale: fast out, slow in, plus scheduled pre-scaling for known peaks
  • Application Insights connected; diagnostic settings to Log Analytics
  • Access restricted to Front Door/App Gateway if one is in front
  • Private endpoints for dependencies, with private DNS zones linked
  • Nothing stateful in-process (session, cache, scheduler, file writes)

🔍 Questions to test yourself

  • How do you achieve zero-downtime deployment on App Service? Deploy to a staging slot, warm it up via the swap warm-up path, verify health, swap (a routing change), verify production, and swap again to roll back.
  • What actually happens during a slot swap? Production's sticky settings are applied to staging, staging restarts with them, Azure warms it up with HTTP requests, then routing flips. The old version stays in staging as your rollback.
  • Which settings swap and which stay? Anything marked "deployment slot setting" stays with the slot — connection strings, environment-specific config, and the managed identity. Everything else follows the code.
  • App Service vs Container Apps vs AKS? Simplicity and slots / containers with KEDA scaling, scale-to-zero and revisions / full Kubernetes when you have a platform team and genuinely need it.
  • What breaks when you scale from 1 to 5 instances? In-memory cache and session, in-process schedulers running five times, SignalR without a backplane, local file writes, and in-process locks.
  • Why is ARR affinity usually wrong? It pins users to instances, unbalancing load and complicating draining — and it hides the real problem, which is in-process state.

Sources: Deployment slots — Microsoft Learn · Slot warm-up guidance — Microsoft Q&A · Blue-green deployments with App Service slots · Zero-downtime releases with slots
